children.blurb: Live testimony cross-referencing applies automated comparison to spoken witness evidence as it is given, checking it against prior depositions, affidavits, exhibits, and other testimony already in the case record.

sections.body: Litigation prediction and judicial analytics is the use of data and machine learning to estimate how courts, judges, opposing counsel, juries, and settlements will behave. In practice, AI systems read dockets, briefs, rulings, and public records to find patterns that a human team might miss. They score judges by ruling history, track counsel by motion practice, and build risk ranges for settlement. They also help lawyers prepare for jury selection and cross-examination by linking testimony to documents and prior statements. The site tracks 146 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which gives this section a live set of disputes to study. The work is not about replacing legal judgment, but about giving it better inputs.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature: docket parsing, citation checking, and basic outcome statistics are reliable when the underlying records are clean and complete. Judicial analytics can show tendencies, but it cannot predict a specific ruling with certainty, because judges respond to facts, arguments, and local rules that data may not capture. Settlement valuation models produce ranges, not answers, and they depend on assumptions about damages, fees, and risk tolerance. Jury selection tools can flag correlations, yet they raise privacy and fairness concerns, and many courts limit what can be used. Live testimony cross-referencing is promising but fragile, because speech recognition, speaker identification, and real-time legal context are hard to combine without error. The honest limit is that prediction is probabilistic, and legal outcomes often turn on human choices that no dataset fully records.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section build from the bench outward. Judicial Analytics covers how judges are profiled and where those profiles help or mislead. Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns looks at the other side's filing habits, timing, and procedural moves. Settlement Valuation and Risk turns those patterns into numerical ranges and scenario models. Jury Selection and Public Data examines how public records and demographics are used to shape a jury pool, along with the ethical lines around that work. Live Testimony Cross-Referencing focuses on the courtroom moment, where transcripts, documents, and prior statements are matched in real time, and a reader would start with Judicial Analytics for the judge, move to Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns for the adversary, then use Settlement Valuation and Risk for the money question, Jury Selection and Public Data for the jury, and Live Testimony Cross-Referencing for trial.
